title: The things we bring to the table
text:
The things we bring to the table
From Grandma’s broccoli casserole to a rowdy game of Turkey Bowl,
five writers reflect on the people, dishes, and traditions that make Thanksgiving. 
It’s not Thanksgiving without Turkey Bowl.
When I first joined my now-husband’s family for Thanksgiving, I was prepared to feast. I wasn’t prepared for the intense game of football that followed. Good thing I brought my stretchy pants.
Turkey Bowl is a beloved tradition in my husband’s New York town. The menfolk gather on the high school football field the day after Thanksgiving for a raucous round of two-hand touch. Some sport their jerseys of old, others raggedy sweatbands; everyone has a few more creaks and groans than in their glory days.
Me? I was just happy to join, even if I was the only female on the field. My opponents lumbered after me, but my spry nature lent itself well to dipping and dodging. And my competitive streak offered its advantages: Someone twice my size accused me of playing too rough. I was so proud.
But alas, all good things must come to an end, as the saying goes. I leaped up to intercept the ball, pivoted abruptly, and – yikes! Twisted my ankle in the soggy turf. My cheeks grew bright red as I got carried off the field by a strapping Australian firefighter, one of my husband’s old classmates. I suppose there are worse ways to end a game.
Every year, I’m invited back to join the shenanigans. These days, I’ll happily cheer from the sidelines. After all, I can’t count on a strapping firefighter to carry me off the field every year. – Samantha Laine Perfas
***
It’s not Thanksgiving without my grandma’s heritage Thanksgiving stuffing.
My family’s stuffing recipe has an unusual ingredient: pimiento-stuffed green olives. Their briny tang cuts through the richness of the gravy, while their green and red colors brighten the otherwise beige Thanksgiving plate. And they’re fun to pick out of the stuffing when no one is looking. The recipe is so beloved that it’s always the first dish to disappear.
My grandmother’s family came from Tucson, Arizona. Through old family photographs and historical documents, I discovered that her ancestors had lived there since Arizona was part of Mexico. Grandma inherited the stuffing recipe from her mother, passed it on to my mom, and then to me.
Whenever I make it, I feel connected to family gatherings stretching back several generations. I plan to pass this treasured recipe on to my two daughters.
Sonoran Mexican cooking often brings savory and sweet flavors together. I like to think of this as a reflection of life itself: joyful moments alongside bitter ones. After all, a full life contains both.
I’m reminded of this as I slowly sauté diced onions in butter until they turn translucent and sweet, and then add the sharp, briny olives at the end.
Every Thanksgiving, this simple dish brings my family’s past to our present. And knowing my daughters love it, too, makes me hopeful it will find a place at their tables someday. – Tia Welch Maerz
***
It’s not Thanksgiving without chana masala and baingan ka bharta.
Thanksgiving, like many holidays I’ve adopted in the United States, has helped me find my own meaning of “Americanness.”
When I arrived in the United States two decades ago, Thanksgiving felt warm and welcoming, yet disorienting. As a vegan, I wasn’t always sure what I could eat. At my first Thanksgiving potluck, I brought what I knew best: chana masala. One guest remarked that it “wasn’t the dish to bring to a Thanksgiving potluck.” Maybe it wasn’t.
The following year, I hosted my own dinner, setting out what I thought was an appropriately American spread: mashed potatoes, green beans, sweet potatoes, cranberry sauce, and apple pie. Unable to serve turkey, I made my signature chana masala the centerpiece. Its tangy spices and aroma of garam masala mingled beautifully with the milder sides, making the meal feel both American and like home.
As friends gathered around the table, one asked, “Why isn’t your homemade baingan ka bharta on the table?” The smoky Indian eggplant dish had clearly earned its place, too.
Now, every year, I prepare traditional vegan Thanksgiving favorites alongside the dishes that connect me to my roots. Chana masala and baingan ka bharta are as much a part of our Thanksgiving as cranberry sauce.
Somewhere between the cranberry sauce and the garam masala, I found a Thanksgiving that feels entirely my own. – Kalpana Jain
***
It’s not Thanksgiving without my grandmother’s broccoli casserole.
I’m not a foodie. Never have been. Everyone knows this about me. I’m a vegetarian who doesn’t like vegetables. I barely cook.
When I was little, my grandmother was the chef in our house. She struggled to find things I liked to eat. But come Thanksgiving, I was super excited about her meal – not for the turkey, not for the stuffing. No, my favorite dish was Gommy’s broccoli casserole.
I looked forward to it every year. Everyone was amazed because I would actually ask for seconds – the only time I ever did that. And it even had a vegetable in it! Granted, it was smothered in cream of mushroom soup, several cups of mayonnaise, and loads of cheddar cheese.
I still make it for holiday meals, and some of my friends actually like it, too. They even ask me to make it. But my foodie husband? He won’t touch it with a 10-foot pole! – Melanie Stetson Freeman
***
It’s not Thanksgiving without a story.
In the closing lines of “A River Runs Through It,” Norman Maclean writes, “Eventually, all things merge into one, ... and some of the words are theirs.”
Maclean’s reflection on the timelessness of family memories brings me back to the Thanksgiving tables of my childhood.
Every table needs a storyteller. In our family, that was my grandfather. All these years later, what I remember most about him are his words.
His stories almost always began in his boyhood home in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, one of America’s last great wilderness areas, where, as I once read, “the towns seem not very successful attempts to hold back the forest.”
He told delightful tales of wandering the forested shores of Lake Superior and of weather rolling off its mighty waters. His stories brought to life blueberry pickers and lumberjacks, copper mines and railroads, freighters on the horizon, and his journey east in search of work during the Great Depression.
His travels across America as a young man made the geography and history we studied in school come alive.
For those of us who once gathered around those Thanksgiving tables, I imagine his stories still come to mind, wherever we are today. Perhaps we even retell a few.
My grandfather still has a place at our table. After all, his words are part of our story, too. – Jim Meddleton
